title: Abdominal electrical stimulation and hand cycling study
official: Home-based abdominal functional electrical stimulation combined with arm-crank exercise to improve respiratory and bowel function and posture in spinal cord injury – a proof-of-concept study
summary:
Background and study aims
Bowel management, trunk control and breathing are often affected after spinal cord injury (SCI), which can reduce quality of life and independence. This study aims to test a new home-based treatment that combines electrical stimulation of the abdominal muscles with arm-crank exercise delivered through live online classes. This study is being ran to find out whether this treatment can improve bowel management, trunk control and breathing in people who have been living with SCI for at least 12 months.

Who can participate? 
People aged 16 years or older who have a cervical or thoracic SCI (at or above T8) for at least 12 months and have sufficient arm strength to use an arm-crank exercise bike.

What does the study involve?
The study involves 12 weeks of home-based electrical stimulation and arm-crank exercise. Participants will join live online exercise classes with other participants and a class leader three times a week for 12 weeks. Each class lasts 60 minutes.

The study is testing two types of electrical stimulation. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive one of the two types. Participants will also need to visit the University of Birmingham twice for assessments: once before starting the programme and once after completing the 12 weeks.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Possible benefits: Regular exercise may improve cardiovascular fitness, while electrical stimulation combined with exercise may help improve trunk control, breathing and bowel management. However, these benefits are not guaranteed.
Possible risks: Electrical stimulation may cause skin irritation or breakdown and, in some individuals with SCI, may trigger autonomic dysreflexia (a sudden and potentially dangerous rise in blood pressure). Exercise may also cause muscle soreness or other muscle and joint discomfort.

Where is the study run from? 
The University of Birmingham, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
March 2027 to December 2028.

Who is funding the study? 
The INSPIRE Foundation, UK

Who is the main contact?
Dr Shin-Yi (Chloe) Chiou; s.chiou@bham.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age 16 years and older with a stable SCI
2. Diagnosed with cervical or thoracic (at or above the T8 level) and medically stable
3. Time since injury > = 12 months
4. Have sufficient elbow flexor strength to operate an arm-crank ergometer
5. Ability to sit unsupported for 30 seconds
6. Have access to a device and internet connection capable of running Zoom
7. Can provide informed consent and able to understand and follow instructions for assessment and intervention

In addition, healthy adults aged 18 years and older will be included as controls
Exclusion criteria:
1. AIS score D or E
2. A previous history of recurrent episodes of severe autonomic dysreflexia (AD)
3. Absence of abdominal muscle contraction in response to FES
4. Contraindications to FES, brain stimulation, or arm cycling (e.g., implanted devices, cardiac pacemaker, pregnancy, or shoulder instability)
5. Severely Obese participant (> 40 BMI)
6. A lack of understanding of English
7. Exclusion from the outcome measure of intra-abdominal pressure if allergic to latex and/or lidocaine 

Adults with known neurological conditions or contraindications to FES or brain stimulation will not be recruited as the controls.
